title: Ads Management and Serving
seoTitle: Design an Ads Management and Display System for a Social Feed
description: Design ad serving for a social feed — campaign management, targeting, real-time auctions, budget pacing, and impression and click logging.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an Ads Management and Serving System?
blocks.text: Advertisers create campaigns with budgets, targeting and creatives; when a user scrolls their feed, the system picks the best ad for that slot in milliseconds through an auction, shows it, and charges the advertiser — without overspending budgets.

items: Advertisers should be able to create campaigns with targeting (age, location, interests), budget, bid and creatives.
When a feed requests an ad, the system should choose the best eligible ad via an auction.
The system should record impressions and clicks and charge advertisers.
Campaigns should not exceed their daily budgets, and spend should be paced through the day.
The ML model that predicts click-through rates (we treat it as a service).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Ad selection within ~50ms so the feed isn't slowed.
Handle millions of ad requests per second.
Budgets must not be significantly overspent; small overshoot is tolerable.
Impression and click logs must be durable — they're how advertisers are billed.
**Campaign**: advertiser, budget, bid strategy, schedule, status.
**Ad**: creative, targeting criteria, belongs to a campaign.
**Ad request**: user ID, context (placement, device), timestamp.
**Impression / Click**: logged events tied to an ad request ID.

blocks.text: The **Campaign Service** stores campaigns in a relational database. Changes are published so serving systems rebuild their in-memory **ad index** within seconds.
2) Choose the best ad for a feed slot

items: **Retrieve**: the ad index (an inverted index from targeting attributes to ads) returns the few thousand ads eligible for this user.
**Rank**: a model predicts click probability; expected value = bid × predicted CTR (plus quality signals).
**Auction**: the highest score wins; with a second-price-style rule, the winner pays just enough to beat the runner-up.
Check that the winning campaign still has budget to spend, then return the creative with a signed impression token.

blocks.text: The client reports impressions when the ad is actually visible; clicks go through a redirect endpoint. Events are written to Kafka, deduplicated by token, and aggregated for billing and reporting.
A **Budget Service** tracks spend per campaign and decides, for each auction, whether a campaign should participate, so spend is spread across the day instead of being exhausted in the first hour.
1) How do we pick an ad within 50ms?

blocks.title: Score every ad for every request

approach.text: Run the CTR model across all active ads.

challenges.text: Millions of ads × millions of requests per second is impossible.

approach.text: An in-memory inverted index (sharded across serving nodes, rebuilt from the campaign stream) narrows millions of ads to a few thousand by targeting. A cheap model trims that to hundreds; an expensive model ranks the final candidates. Cache user features close to the serving nodes.

challenges.text: Index freshness: paused campaigns must disappear within seconds, so updates stream in rather than waiting for a rebuild.

blocks.text: 2) How do we avoid overspending budgets?

blocks.title: Check the database on every auction

approach.text: Read and update the campaign's spend in the database per impression.

challenges.text: A popular campaign gets thousands of impressions per second — a hot row and slow auctions.

approach.text: A central budget service hands each serving node a small **spend allowance** per campaign for the next few seconds and tracks actual spend from the impression stream. Nodes decide locally from their allowance (no network call per auction). A pacing controller throttles participation probability so spend tracks a target curve through the day.

challenges.text: Allowances create small overshoot when many nodes spend at once; keep allowances small near the end of a budget.

quiz.question: Why use multi-stage retrieval and ranking?
options: Scoring every ad per request is impossible within ~50ms
quiz.explanation: Cheap filters narrow candidates before expensive models run.

quiz.question: What score typically decides the auction?
options: Bid times predicted click-through rate (plus quality)
quiz.explanation: Expected value balances price and relevance.

quiz.question: How can serving nodes enforce budgets without a database call per auction?
options: Use small spend allowances handed out by a budget service
quiz.explanation: Local allowances bound overspend while avoiding hot rows.

quiz.question: What is budget pacing for?
options: Spreading spend across the day instead of exhausting it early
quiz.explanation: Pacing gives campaigns delivery throughout the day.
